newsitem.title: USA: Some buy-siders to shed stocks post-U.S. rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Some buy-siders to shed stocks post-U.S. rate hike.

text.p: Some U.S. money managers said they will lighten the equity component of portfolios under management in reaction to the rise in key interest rates by Federal Reserve policymakers on Tuesday.
However, others said for now they will stick to present allocations despite expectations for a bumpy ride.

Fixed income portfolio managers said government and corporate debt markets had largely anticipated and priced in the 25-basis-point rise in the federal funds rate and have no immediate plans to alter their asset mix.
But some advisors said they will continue to shorten their portfolio's overall duration -- a measure of the average maturity of a series of cash flows.

"I will probably be selling equities over the course of the next couple weeks," said a U.S. money manager who runs a sizeable garden-variety hedge fund comprised mostly of high-grade corporate bonds, stocks, and Group of Seven currencies.

"I am personally of the view that this is the first of a few rate moves we may be getting over the next six months to a year ... and I would suspect the stock market in the United States has seen its high for the next six months or year," the manager said.
He added that the use of proceeds from equity sales will be held in cash and cash equivalents over the short term.
Others were not as convinced Tuesday's rate hike was the first of many and thus do not believe the spectacular run-up in U.S. equity markets has peaked.

"I don't know if I buy the notion that since there is this one, there will be a lot more," said Kirk Hartman, executive vice president and chief investment officer of West Coast Investment Management Group, Bank of America.
"I still think the (Dow Jones Industrials index) is going to bounce around between 6,500 and 7,000 this year," he added.

Hartman said he has no immediate plans to change his current allocation of 55 percent stocks and 45 percent fixed income, a mix he called "not terribly aggressive." He expects the 30-year Treasury bond yield to stay between 6.50 and 7.25 percent in 1997.
"I would be very surprised, even with the tightening, if the long bond (yield) went over 7.25 percent," he said.
International fund managers interviewed said they had no plans to change their regional portfolio weightings with respect to well accepted benchmarks as a result of higher U.S. rates.

"(The rise) will not have any effect; it is very heavily discounted. We are pretty much set up with that assumption that the U.S. bond markets will probably come into a little bit of pressure later on this year," said Robert Kowit, vice president, global fixed income at Federated Investors.

"It becomes a question of how much duration and exposure do we have," he asked. Kowit said he decreased his emerging market funds' Brady bond duration exposure over the last two months, in part due to higher rate expectations and also the tightness of Brady yield spreads.
Kowit said it was "pretty safe" to say this last rate hike would not be a one-off and he sees the federal funds rate rising 50 to 75 basis points in total this cycle.

Brian Gendreau, international economist at JP Morgan and Co Inc, said fixed income money managers there had been expecting a Fed rate hike for some time, adding that they will not alter allocations bar an unexpected market reaction.
"The only thing that would make us change our view ... is if we have a really violent sell-off in the Treasury market and 10-year yields go through the roof," he said, adding it was unlikely.

Treasuries and U.S. stocks rose modestly in a knee-jerk reaction to the news, only to shed all gains shortly after. The dollar briefly spiked lower versus the mark but soon recovered to above its pre-announcement level. Against the yen, the dollar crawled higher after an initial dip.
Gendreau said he continues to recommend that clients shorten their portfolio's duration or move into cash.
"It is a global bear market already. The European markets have sold off and what we are recommending is that people go short duration," he said.
Gendreau added that "in the very short-term," economic weakness in Japan makes Japanese Government Bonds a somewhat attractive investment relative to Treasuries.
((N.A. Treasuries Desk, 212-859-1677))
